subject: i) spatial trends and  ii) irregular sampling times for "ar1" model

messages.author: 4c16af0e8fc1c8fa
messages.subject: i) spatial trends and  ii) irregular sampling times for "ar1" model
parts:
Thank you for all the wonderful feedback provided on this forum.
I have two questions, apologies in advance if they are hopelessly naive.

1) Is is possible to estimate spatial trends along with the spatial random effects with spde models?

My data has a strong latitudinal trend which quantifying is of interest, though there is much more spatial variability than just a latitudinal trend. I understand confounding is a possible issue but do not know precisely how to deal with it.

2) If I have sampling data that occurred every other year and I want to estimate a spatial-temporal "ar1" model. What is the best way of doing that such the ar coefficient can be on an annual basis?

thank you!

messages.author: 9940b4fcc153c7d7
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] i) spatial trends and ii) irregular sampling times for "ar1" model
parts:
Hi,

1) With several spatial replicates, you can identify what is a trend and what is randomness. 

With no spatial replicates, this is notoriously difficult to understand, and your result depends quite strongly on your model assumptions and priors.

Ask yourself the question: "Can I be sure that it is this covariate which drives my observations?". If you have latitudinal trend, it is difficult to know which of the many potential latitudinal covariates that are the true cause of your trend. You see what I mean?

An approach I like is fixing the spatial range to different values and doing a scenario analysis. The idea goes: "If the unmeasured covariates and spatial noise is of range 1km, then the fixed effect is significant, and if the range is ... then ..., but if... then ..." (This approach needs one INLA call for each fixed value of the range.)

2) I think there is a section of the spde tutorial that explains how to have a mesh in time. Then the ar coefficient can be yearly, but you only have a time-mesh every second year (where you have data).

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka
